subjects.displayTitle: Addressing Christians: the challenge of recognition
subjects.introduction: What would it mean for an answer to a cherished promise to arrive in an unfamiliar form? These addresses to Christians make that question immediate through images of opened gates, the human heart as a temple, and a renewed summons from heaven. Their central claim is Bahá’í: fidelity to Christ calls for recognition of a further revelation. Reading John’s account of the Spirit of truth alongside them gives the promise its Gospel setting and makes the interpretive question more precise [1]. The neighboring subjects of Christ’s return and differences of understanding invite both sustained inquiry and restraint in disagreement. An attentive reading can hear the urgency of the proclamation while taking seriously the convictions of those to whom it is addressed.
subjects.arc: Open with the living human temple, develop the summons to recognition, and bring scriptural promises into conversation with response, suffering, and service.

subjects.displayTitle: Addressing Jews: covenant, promise, and recognition
subjects.introduction: Mountains, a throne, a burning tree, and a renewed covenant become voices of expectation in these addresses to Jews. The selections proclaim Bahá’u’lláh through the remembered language of Abraham, Moses, David, and the prophets, moving between glad tidings and searching challenges to recognition. Isaiah’s vision of righteous judgment, safety, and knowledge of God offers a primary Jewish scriptural setting in which to explore the substance of prophetic hope [1]. The neighboring addresses to Christians and Muslims raise a shared question: how can devotion to an inherited revelation shape the encounter with a later claim? These are Bahá’í interpretations of fulfillment, inviting examination alongside Jewish readings of the same scriptures, whose meanings should be heard on their own terms.
subjects.arc: Begin with the call from Carmel to Zion, follow covenantal and prophetic images, and move from joyful announcement to the work of recognition.

subjects.displayTitle: Addressing Muslims: scripture, fairness, and response
subjects.introduction: A reader can cherish a sacred book and still face a demanding question about how to judge a new religious claim. These addresses to Muslims press that question through appeals to the Qur’án, the appearance of divine signs, freedom from self-interest, and the day of judgment. They speak from the claims of the Báb and Bahá’u’lláh; their urgency belongs to an encounter involving real differences of belief. Qur’án 29:46 contributes a related discipline for conversation with the People of the Book: the best manner of engagement and acknowledgment of the one God [1]. Read alongside the subject of Muhammad as the Seal of the Prophets, this compilation invites careful attention both to the evidence offered and to the fairness with which any response is formed.
subjects.arc: Begin with the responsibility of fair judgment, examine the appeal to scripture, and then hear the proclamations and warnings that make response urgent.

It supplies an Islamic scriptural resource for thinking about how religious disagreement is conducted. subjects.displayTitle: The return of Christ: expectation and recognition
subjects.introduction: How would we recognize a return whose meaning exceeded the picture we had formed of it? These selections approach Christ’s return through clouds, heaven, renewed spiritual power, and the example of Elijah and John the Baptist. They set out a Bahá’í understanding of continuity in the divine reality of the Manifestations, culminating in explicit claims concerning the Báb and Bahá’u’lláh. Acts preserves the promise of Jesus’ return in the setting of his ascension [1], while Matthew presents the disciples recognizing an Elijah connection in John [2]. Reading these passages together opens a careful inquiry into identity, symbolism, and fulfillment. The neighboring subjects of proclamation and individual understanding keep the inquiry connected to how people encounter and discuss a claim.

subjects.displayTitle: The Seal of the Prophets: finality and fulfillment
subjects.introduction: A seal can bring a profound question into focus: what has been completed, and what does completion mean for the future? These selections repeatedly honor Muhammad as the Seal of the Prophets while interpreting the consummation of a prophetic cycle in relation to a promised day of divine revelation. They invite readers to hold together affirmation and interpretation rather than passing quickly over their tension. Qur’án 33:40 and the final-brick image in Sahih al-Bukhari give the language of finality its own Islamic scriptural and traditional force [1] [2]. Read alongside Christ’s return and the addresses to Muslims, the compilation opens a demanding inquiry into continuity, expectation, and the reasons different religious communities understand fulfillment differently.
subjects.arc: Begin with honor for Muhammad, place explicit statements of finality together, and then work through the compilation’s account of consummation and renewed revelation.

subjects.displayTitle: Christian teachings and practices: belief brought into life
subjects.introduction: What happens when the language of faith is measured against the life it produces? This compilation moves from the practice of Christ’s teachings to spiritual nourishment, doctrinal disagreement, and criticism of ecclesiastical customs and power. Many selections are reported conversations containing compressed historical or theological accounts; their source labels matter, and the collection does not supply a complete history of Christianity. Reading the Chalcedonian definition of Christ and the Catholic explanation of Eucharistic presence allows two traditions of doctrine to speak in their own precise language [1] [2]. Alongside the neighboring study of individual understanding, these readings invite scrutiny of both conduct and interpretation: how convictions are expressed, how disagreements are represented, and how religious life becomes a source of love rather than contention.
subjects.arc: Begin with teachings put into practice, explore spiritual nourishment and doctrine, and then examine the relationships among custom, authority, disagreement, and renewal.

references.label: 1 · Definition of Chalcedon (451), in Schaff’s Creeds of Christendom
references.note: Read the definition itself, distinguishing it from the editor’s extensive notes. It affirms one Christ, fully divine and fully human, with the two natures united without confusion or division. Compare this precise formulation with the compilation’s compressed descriptions of Christian beliefs. It is a particular doctrinal statement, not an account of every Christian community or an invitation to erase differences with Bahá’í interpretation.

references.label: 2 · Catechism of the Catholic Church, §§1374–1376
references.note: These paragraphs explain Catholic belief in Christ’s substantial Eucharistic presence and attribute the sacramental transformation to Christ and the Holy Spirit; the priest’s words act through divine power. Read this account beside the selections about spiritual food and priestly claims. It helps distinguish the doctrine’s own account of agency from a critic’s description, while leaving substantive differences available for discussion.

subjects.displayTitle: Persecution of Christians: faith, power, and endurance
subjects.introduction: Why can a community with little public power become a source of enduring spiritual influence? These selections recall the trials of Christ and the apostles, examine the obstruction of prejudice and status, and consider courage under opposition. Their historical allusions range across periods; one retained account concerns a Bahá’í family’s suffering, making the analogy across communities part of the reading. Acts offers a particularly fruitful comparison in Gamaliel, a Pharisee who counsels restraint toward the apostles [1]. His presence helps readers resist turning accounts of particular opponents into judgments upon an entire people. Alongside the subjects of proclamation and religious practice, the compilation invites reflection on steadfastness, humane judgment, and the difference between spiritual influence and the possession of worldly authority.
subjects.arc: Begin with the unexpected power of ordinary disciples, consider the costs and causes of opposition, and widen the inquiry toward restraint and comparisons across religious experience.

references.label: 1 · Acts 5:33–39 (King James Version)
references.note: Faced with a council considering the apostles’ deaths, Gamaliel, identified as a Pharisee and teacher of the law, urges caution and counsels leaving them alone lest opposition become a struggle against God. The passage both opens a question about uncertainty and power and shows why a religious community must not be treated as a single uniform actor.

subjects.introduction: People can speak about the same sacred figure and understand that figure differently. This brief reported conversation uses differing accounts of Christ to explore conscience, comprehension, and the damage of quarrelling. Its point invites reflection on how disagreement is conducted even when participants retain convictions about truth. Paul’s counsel concerning disputed food and holy days offers a comparison in another setting: believers are asked to refrain from despising and judging one another [1]. Read beside the more extensive subjects of Christian teachings and Christ’s return, this single selection provides a pause for considering whether inquiry can deepen understanding while preserving fellowship.
subjects.arc: Read the single passage as a concentrated reflection on understanding, conscience, and the manner of disagreement.

references.label: 1 · Romans 14:1–6 (King James Version)
references.note: Paul addresses disputes over food and the observance of days, urging believers to welcome one another and refrain from contempt or judgment. The subjects of disagreement differ, so the passage should not be treated as declaring all doctrinal claims equivalent; the comparison concerns the conduct of people who remain in disagreement.
